headline: Black people who built and ran computing
summary: Black computing history includes operators, researchers, educators and professional networks. These records show different routes into technical work, including a training program with reported internship outcomes.
coverageNote: Five documented episodes in U.S. computing. They establish particular jobs, credentials and programs, not an unbroken chain to every software, systems or reliability role.
question: Which appointment, training or advancement record connects Black workers to your exact role and employer?

events.title: Joe Thompson enters computing through paid work at MIT
events.decisionMaker: MIT's Whirlwind project; the museum account does not name the hiring official.
events.barrier: The Computer History Museum identifies Thompson as the first Black employee on Whirlwind's early staff.
events.change: MIT recruited him into a route combining study with paid nighttime work operating and programming Whirlwind.
events.outcome: He later programmed SAGE at RAND and eventually advanced to branch leadership during his career.
events.limit: This establishes operations and programming work, not a modern DevOps or SRE title or a direct connection to your employer.

source.title: Computer History Museum · Trailblazers and Change Agents
source.locator: Joe Thompson: First Generation Programmer; museum account and linked collection

events.title: Clarence Ellis earns a computer-science doctorate
events.decisionMaker: University of Illinois, the degree-granting institution.
events.barrier: The university identifies Ellis as the first Black American to earn a computer-science PhD; it does not document a specific admissions rule he changed.
events.change: Ellis completed doctoral work while contributing to the ILLIAC IV supercomputer's hardware, software and applications.
events.outcome: His subsequent work included leading the PARC group that developed Officetalk, a system for remote collaboration.
events.limit: His credential and technical leadership are documented individual achievements, not proof that doctoral access or hiring became equal.

source.title: University of Illinois · Clarence “Skip” Ellis
source.locator: 2019 Distinguished Achievement Memorial Award biography, opening three paragraphs

events.title: Howard builds a formal computer-science route
events.people: Howard University's students, faculty and academic leadership
events.decisionMaker: Howard University; the college history does not name the approving official or a single founding year.
events.barrier: Howard describes educating Black engineers as its institutional mission; this account does not document individual students' admissions barriers.
events.change: The university inaugurated a computer-science program during the 1970–1980 period and integrated it into its engineering school.
events.outcome: Computing became an established field of study within Howard's academic structure.
events.limit: The history verifies program development, not graduate placement totals or a hiring relationship with a particular employer.

source.title: Howard University College of Engineering and Architecture · Our History
source.locator: Paragraphs covering the 1970–1997 school structure and programs inaugurated in the 1970–1980 era

events.title: Jesse Bemley and BDPA create a student programming route
events.people: Dr. Jesse Bemley and Black Data Processing Associates members
events.decisionMaker: BDPA established its student education program; its history credits Bemley with founding the high-school computer competition.
events.barrier: BDPA organized practical technical education and professional connections for aspiring students; this source does not measure each participant's prior access.
events.change: Students could develop programming and application-building skills through chapter training and a national competition.
events.outcome: BDPA reports that the program has exposed tens of thousands of high-school students to coding and offered routes to scholarships.
events.limit: That is the organization's reported educational reach, not independently verified job-placement or promotion data.

source.title: BDPA · About Us
source.locator: Our History; What Does BDPA Offer? → High School Programs

events.title: Howard West connects study with an engineering workplace
events.people: Howard students, Howard faculty and Google engineers
events.decisionMaker: Howard University and Google jointly ran the Howard West pilot.
events.barrier: The partnership addressed access to applied computer-science study and professional experience for students from historically Black institutions.
events.change: The 2017 pilot provided a three-month computer-science education program at Google.
events.outcome: In September 2018, Google reported that 26 students completed the pilot and half had obtained engineering internships at Google or elsewhere in the industry.
events.limit: This is Google's report of one cohort. Internships are not permanent jobs, and participation is not evidence of a connection to an individual reader.

source.title: Google · Tech Exchange brings Black and Latinx students to Google
source.locator: September 18, 2018; paragraph beginning 'The institutions sending students to Google this year'
